transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-10-29 15:00 PT; Duration: ~52m; Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Ava (Redwood SE), Lena (Peregrine CTO), Markus (Platform), Nikolai (ML), Priyanka (Infra)

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros — I'm Samir from Redwood, AE. Ava is our solutions engineer.
[00:08] Lena: Hi all, Lena here. We'll be driving the integration on our side. Markus, Nikolai and Priyanka are on the call.
[00:15] Markus: hey.
[00:17] Ava: great to meet you all. quick agenda — understand your stack, integration points (SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex), and tradeoffs for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.
[00:27] Nikolai: yeah, thanks. we're evaluating how to replace some of our in-house gateway stuff and also want to centralize inference across teams.
[00:34] Samir: perfect, can you give a quick picture of current architecture and pain points?
[00:39] Markus: sure. so currently we run a Node gateway that fans requests to a mix of vendor endpoints. We have a caching layer and some custom batching logic but it's brittle — KV cache mostly in Redis, though we call it K-V cash in the docs, ha. Our main pain: unpredictable latency when vendor endpoints throttle, and costs spiking on peak.
[00:56] Priyanka: also we need SOC2-ready audit trails and want KMS integration for keys — and some customers require data not to leave the VPC.
[01:06] Samir: got it. Redwood has a few ways to approach this — hosted API for fastest time-to-value, Dedicated for predictable perf and reserved capacity, and Private for VPC/on-prem. Ava, maybe walk through integration options?
[01:17] Ava: yeah. on the SDK side we support python and node officially, and there's a Go community client. We also provide adapter examples for LangChain and LlamaIndex — sometimes transcription labels those as "LongChain" or "Llama idx" but they're the standard connectors. For gateway patterns we see two common approaches: lightweight sidecar proxy per service, or an edge gateway that fronts teams. Sidecar keeps latency low and localizes KV cache. Edge gateway centralizes policies and quotas.
[01:42] Markus: how hard is it to swap in the Redwood SDK? we have a lot of LangChain pipelines in python.
[01:49] Ava: pretty straightforward. LangChain's llm wrapper can call Redwood endpoints with the SDK; we have a sample repo that shows streaming tokens, function calling, and structured outputs. For LlamaIndex we have a connector that maps index queries to Redwood embeddings and generative calls.
[02:05] Nikolai: any gotchas with KV cache or prefix caching when using long-context models? our assistants depend on pretty large context windows.
[02:12] Ava: we surface KV cache controls in the SDK — but the runtime handles KV eviction and efficient KV cache reuse. People sometimes mishear it as K V cash, but the point is the same: we keep a persistent KV cache to reduce re-computation. If you do sidecar, the cache can be local and shared with your service which helps latency.
[02:30] Lena: on compliance: Private deployment — does that mean Redwood's control plane is separate? what about audit logs and KMS?
[02:39] Samir: yes. Private deployments let you run the data plane in your VPC, optionally air-gapped. The control plane can be customer-managed or we can run a private control plane. We support KMS integrations and HSM for key management, and audit logs can be shipped to your SIEM. We'll send the full security pack after the call.
[02:55] Priyanka: good. we also need SAML/SSO and RBAC.
[02:59] Ava: supported — SAML, SCIM provisioning, role-based roles etc.
[03:04] Markus: back to rate limits: we have bursty traffic (e.g., summary jobs) — how do quotas work and what about per-route SLAs?
[03:12] Samir: Redwood exposes per-token quotas, per-route quotas and token budgets per API key. For Dedicated, you can set reserved throughput and burst capacity; for Hosted we have tiered rps limits and token quotas. There's also automatic fallback: if a model variant is out of capacity we can route to a compatible variant, which reduces errors.
[03:30] Nikolai: when you say model variant fallback, will that change cost or output quality drastically? we care about regression.
[03:36] Ava: yes it can affect both. Redwood Optimize suggests quantization and model selection based on workload. We also integrate quality monitoring — you can tie prompt sets to evals so if a fallback causes a regression you get an alert. People often tie that into their CI for rollouts.
[03:51] Lena: we run many LangChain chains with tools and function calls. How does Redwood handle streaming and function calling?
[03:59] Ava: streaming is available in the SDK; we stream tokens as they are generated. Function calling is supported; the SDK can return structured JSON that LangChain can parse directly. There's occasional mis-annotation in transcripts where "function" becomes "funtion", but it's fully supported.
[04:13] Markus: curious about observability — we want per-token cost and latency breakdown per route and pin it to traces. what are the hooks?
[04:21] Samir: Redwood Console provides token-level cost breakdowns, per-route dashboards, traces that integrate with OpenTelemetry. We have trace-id propagation — you can push Redwood trace ids into Jaeger/Datadog/Sentry. The SDK emits metrics and you can attach correlation IDs.
[04:34] Priyanka: and sampling? we don't want every single token in traces.
[04:37] Ava: sampling and log redaction are supported. You can set retention policies in Console and send only aggregated metrics to your monitoring.
[04:45] Lena: integration into our gateway — we have a custom auth layer and our own quota enforcement. Does Redwood's gateway replace that, or do we keep ours and use Redwood as a backend?
[04:53] Samir: both patterns are common. If you want Redwood to enforce quotas centrally, you can use an edge gateway pattern. If you want to keep auth and policy local, a sidecar that talks to Redwood endpoints is typical. Sidecar reduces network hops. Also in Dedicated you get reserved GPUs which helps with latency-sensitive endpoints.
[05:10] Markus: what about SDK languages — Go was community; is it production-ready?
[05:15] Ava: the Go client is stable for common flows, but we prioritize python/node first. For Go we have samples and we're iterating. If Go is critical we can prioritize fixes during a POC.
[05:25] Nikolai: can we do local inference with Redwood Private? some models we need to keep on-prem for residency.
[05:30] Samir: yes Private supports on-prem deployments. The runtime is the same, we provide the orchestration and you'll have the option to run the control plane in your network. There's a packaging step and it's a longer onboarding than Hosted.
[05:42] Lena: tradeoffs — if we start Hosted to iterate and then move to Dedicated or Private, how painful is the migration?
[05:48] Ava: we've designed the API and SDK to be identical across modes. Most customers prototype on Hosted, then switch to Dedicated or Private by updating endpoint configs and provisioning capacity. Rollouts, canaries and model pinning are supported.
[06:00] Markus: cost — can you give a rough comparison for our workload? we expect 300 qps average, spikes to 1.2k qps for short bursts, and large context sizes.
[06:09] Samir: we'll put detailed numbers in the pricing worksheet. high level: Hosted is pay-as-you-go (per-token), Dedicated is reserved capacity that drops unit cost for steady throughput, and Private adds a platform fee. For your burst profile you might use Dedicated with burst pool or Hosted plus a burst plan. We'll model it in the spreadsheet.
[06:26] Nikolai: how do rate limits interact with LangChain retries? we sometimes have built-in retries in the orchestration.
[06:32] Ava: good question. SDKs expose retry hooks and idempotency keys; we recommend exponential backoff plus client-side rate limiting to avoid hitting vendor-side throttles. If you use sidecar, the sidecar can issue token bucket-based local throttles.
[06:45] Lena: any reg on data retention? we have PII in prompts occasionally.
[06:50] Samir: data retention policies are configurable. On Dedicated and Private you can set zero retention for user data, and we support encryption at rest and in transit. We'll include the retention matrix.
[06:59] Markus: one more — can Redwood integrate with our event bus for async inference? we have jobs queued in Kafka.
[07:06] Ava: yes — you can use the SDK in workers to pull jobs and call Redwood. Batching is supported server-side, and you can also batch on the client. For high-throughput async jobs, Dedicated is usually recommended.
[07:18] Nikolai: about the LangChain adapter — does it support tool/agent flows or just simple llm calls?
[07:23] Ava: it supports tool flows; we've got examples that wire Redwood LLM calls into LangChain agents, including streaming tool results. Some of those examples are in our demo repo.
[07:33] Markus: logging + troubleshooting — in case of degraded quality after a rollout, what traces do we get?
[07:39] Samir: you get per-request traces, token deltas, model and kernel selection metadata. We also log model variant decisions and fallback reasons. If a rollout triggers regressions you can link eval sets and get alerts.
[07:53] Lena: I noticed a mention of "kernel selection" in your docs — is that something we need to think about?
[07:58] Ava: kernel selection is internal to the runtime — it picks optimized kernels/kernels for hardware and sequence length. Customers don't manage it manually, but we surface some controls (quantization profiles, preferred kernels) if you need deterministic performance.
[08:12] Samir: we want to highlight a pattern here — for teams with strict VPC + compliance, Private with a dedicated control plane and KMS is common. For teams moving fast, Hosted + SDK + sidecar is fastest. Dedicated is the middle ground for cost predictability.
[08:26] Priyanka: what's the expected onboarding timeline for a small POC? we want to validate latency and cost in 2 weeks ideally.
[08:34] Samir: typical POC — week 1: provisioning and sample repo integration, week 2: run benchmarks and adjust config. For Dedicated it's a bit longer to provision GPU pools but a short trial using Hosted could validate perf quickly.
[08:47] Markus: do you provide perf harnesses or load scripts?
[08:50] Ava: yes, we'll provide load scripts, a benchmark harness, and suggested prompt sets. We can also run a joint test where we run your sample traffic against Hosted and a Dedicated estimate.
[08:59] Nikolai: can we get a sample for token-level billing so we can attribute cost to features?
[09:04] Samir: Console provides token breakdowns per key/route. We'll include a sample billing export in the POC folder.
[09:12] Lena: slight tangent — LlamaIndex vs LangChain — our search stack currently uses an index layer. which adapter is better?
[09:20] Ava: both work; LlamaIndex typically handles vector stores and retrieval-augmented generation flows well. Our LlamaIndex connector supports embeddings and retrieval calls; LangChain works better for agent/tool orchestration. We've got examples for both.
[09:34] Markus: any caveats about vector store compatibility? we use Pinecone and an internal vector DB.
[09:40] Ava: embeddings are standard. We output vectors and you can push them to Pinecone or your store. For retrieval latency you might colocate the embedding generation near the vector DB.
[09:50] Priyanka: can we do private peering so traffic never traverses the public internet for Hosted?
[09:55] Samir: Hosted options typically go over the internet, but Dedicated/Private can be VPC peered or on-prem. For strict residency Hosted won't be enough.
[10:04] Lena: OK. let's talk about a concrete POC scope — we want to validate: 1) end-to-end latency on chat flows with 8k context, 2) throughput for async summarization, 3) integration effort for LangChain agent.
[10:17] Samir: perfect. our suggested POC: provision a test account (Hosted initially), run your sample traffic with our harness, then spin up a small Dedicated reserve for comparison. We'll measure p95 latency, cost per 1k tokens, and any regression in outputs.
[10:30] Markus: what's the recommended token batching settings? we currently do client-side batching at 8 requests per batch.
[10:36] Ava: it depends on latency targets. For sub-200ms token latency batching is minimal; for throughput-oriented jobs batching increases throughput and reduces cost. We'll surface recommended batching profiles in the worksheet.
[10:50] Nikolai: edge cases: what if a model upgrade drops quality mid-POC?
[10:53] Ava: you can pin models by version and use canary rollouts. We also have regression alerts if quality metrics drop.
[10:59] Lena: great. any things we should watch for on our side while integrating?
[11:03] Ava: provide realistic prompt sets, correlation IDs, and expected traffic patterns. Also decide early whether you'll do sidecars or an edge gateway — that affects where you put your KV cache.
[11:12] Samir: ok quick recap before we wrap — Samir will send pricing and the reserved capacity worksheet; Ava will share demo repos (LangChain, LlamaIndex, sidecar example), Peregrine will send infra diagram and sample traffic; Priyanka will confirm compliance constraints. We'll target a POC kickoff week of 2026-11-09.
[11:30] Lena: sounds good to me. thanks.
[11:33] Markus: thanks everyone.
[11:35] Samir: thanks all — we'll follow up with the links and schedule.

End of transcript.
